--- title: "Confusion matrix and threshold metrics" description: "Evaluating yes/no decisions: accuracy, precision, recall and why the threshold matters." --- **Question answered:** if we turn the model's probabilities into yes/no decisions, how good are those decisions? ## From probabilities to decisions Our models predict a *probability* of a claim. Many uses need a *decision* instead: inspect this policy or not, refer it to underwriting or not. The usual way to get one is to pick a **threshold** $t$ and predict $$ \hat y = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \hat p \ge t \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} $$ Every metric on this page evaluates **the model together with a threshold**. Change the threshold and all of them change. ## The confusion matrix Comparing decisions with outcomes gives four kinds of cases: | | Predicted 0 | Predicted 1 | |---|---|---| | **Actual 0** | true negative (TN) | false positive (FP), 'false alarm' | | **Actual 1** | false negative (FN), 'miss' | true positive (TP) | Here is the GBM on the 169\,504 test policies at the conventional threshold of 0.5 and at a much lower threshold of 0.05: ::: {#cell-fig-confusion .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.8)) plot_confusion_matrix(c_half, ax=axes[0], title="Threshold 0.5") plot_confusion_matrix(c_low, ax=axes[1], title="Threshold 0.05") fig.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Confusion matrices of the GBM at two thresholds. Color intensity is on a log scale.](confusion-matrix_files/figure-html/fig-confusion-output-1.png){#fig-confusion width=899 height=407} ::: ::: At 0.5, the model flags just 2 policies, and 0 of them had a claim. Its highest predicted probability is only 0\.52: with a claim rate of 3\.7%, very few policies come anywhere near 50%. At 0.05, the model catches 2\,725 of the 6\,236 policies with claims, at the cost of 28\,708 false alarms. ## Metrics derived from the confusion matrix | Metric | Formula | Question it answers | |---|---|---| | Accuracy | $\frac{TP + TN}{N}$ | What share of decisions is correct? | | Precision | $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$ | Of the flagged policies, what share had a claim? | | Recall, true positive rate (TPR), sensitivity | $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$ | Of the policies with a claim, what share did we flag? | | Specificity, true negative rate (TNR) | $\frac{TN}{TN + FP}$ | Of the policies without a claim, what share did we leave alone? | | False positive rate (FPR) | $\frac{FP}{FP + TN} = 1 - \text{TNR}$ | Of the policies without a claim, what share did we flag? | | F1 score | $2 \cdot \frac{\text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}$ | A single summary of precision and recall (their harmonic mean) | | Balanced accuracy | $\frac{\text{TPR} + \text{TNR}}{2}$ | Accuracy if both classes were equally common | Precision and recall look at the positive class from two sides: precision asks how *trustworthy* a flag is, recall how *complete* the flagging is. Raising the threshold usually increases precision and decreases recall. ## The accuracy paradox ::: {#tbl-accuracy-paradox .cell tbl-cap='Threshold metrics at the default threshold 0.5.' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} metrics = ["accuracy", "precision", "recall (TPR)", "specificity (TNR)", "balanced accuracy"] pd.DataFrame({m: threshold_metrics(y, b[m], 0.5)[metrics] for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")}).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
Null GLM GBM
accuracy 0.963 0.963 0.963
precision NaN NaN 0.000
recall (TPR) 0.000 0.000 0.000
specificity (TNR) 1.000 1.000 1.000
balanced accuracy 0.500 0.500 0.500
``` ::: ::: All three models reach an accuracy of about 96\.3%, including the Null model, which never predicts a claim. That number is simply the share of policies *without* a claim. Under class imbalance: - **Accuracy is dominated by the majority class.** 'Always predict 0' reaches 96\.3% without learning anything. - **Always compare with the Null model.** An accuracy only means something next to the accuracy of predicting the majority class (here 96\.3%). - **Balanced accuracy and recall expose the problem**: 0.5 and 0.0 say this decision rule doesn't find any claims. The GBM is not useless, though. The problem is the threshold, not the model. ## Choosing a threshold ::: {#cell-fig-threshold .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4)) plot_score_distributions(y, b["GBM"], ax=axes[0], threshold=0.05) plot_threshold_metrics(y, b["GBM"], ax=axes[1]) fig.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: predicted claim probabilities of the GBM for policies without and with a claim. Right: threshold metrics of the GBM as the threshold moves.](confusion-matrix_files/figure-html/fig-threshold-output-1.png){#fig-threshold width=1086 height=428} ::: ::: The left panel shows why no threshold separates the classes cleanly. Policies with a claim get higher probabilities *on average*, but the two distributions overlap heavily. The right panel shows the resulting trade-off: - **Lowering the threshold** flags more policies. Recall rises and precision falls. - **Accuracy keeps rising with the threshold**, because flagging fewer policies means fewer false alarms among the large majority without claims. Maximizing accuracy pushes towards 'never flag anything'. So which threshold is right? That depends on **what each kind of error costs**, not on the model. If a missed claim costs $c_{FN}$ and a false alarm costs $c_{FP}$, and the probabilities are calibrated, the cost-minimizing rule is to flag a policy when $$ \hat p \ge \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}. $$ For example, if a review costs 50 EUR and catching a claim early saves 950 EUR, the optimal threshold is $50 / (50 + 950) = 0.05$. Decision curves and calibration, covered in later pages, build on this idea. ## Takeaways - Threshold metrics evaluate a **decision rule**, so always report the threshold along with them. - Under class imbalance, **accuracy mostly measures the class balance**. Compare with the Null model, and prefer recall, precision or balanced accuracy. - The threshold should come from the **costs of errors**, not from the 0.5 default. - To judge the model independently of any one threshold, look at all thresholds at once: that is the [ROC curve](roc-auc.qmd).
